summary: A 1977 version of the Telnet Data Entry Terminal option, replacing RFC 731. It is updated by RFC 1043.

eli5.summary: This is the corrected version of the rules for talking to form-style terminals over Telnet.

how does telnet support form filling terminals
subtitle: A Telnet option that lets a host drive a forms-style data entry terminal with cursor, field and transmit controls.

tldr.problem: Telnet was designed for scroll-mode terminals such as the teletype, but users now wanted to run applications on data entry terminals with addressable screens and protected form fields.
tldr.mechanism: The Data Entry Terminal (DET) option, code 20, defines a Network Virtual Data Entry Terminal whose cursor, erase, transmit and format controls are all sent as Telnet subnegotiation subcommands, after the two sides negotiate which facilities they support.
tldr.outcome: RFC 732 replaces RFC 731, and the index lists it as updated by RFC 1043. Its subcommands are verbose, so an appendix suggests using the Byte Macro Option to shrink common ones.

today: RFC 732 obsoletes RFC 731 and the index lists it as updated by RFC 1043; its status is recorded as unknown.

sections.title: Why a Data Entry Terminal Option
sections.content:
Telnet was first designed for scroll-mode terminals. As the Network grew into production use, users wanted facilities it did not offer. The Data Entry Terminal (DET) option, Telnet option code 20, defines a Network Virtual Data Entry Terminal (NVDET): a keyboard that can generate all ASCII characters plus optional function keys, and a rectangular screen M characters wide by N lines high.

The option puts every terminal control inside Telnet subnegotiations rather than in the data stream, so a program that knows its terminal can still send raw characters for functions the option does not cover. Peripheral devices such as printers are out of scope and are left to a separate option. Defaults are WON'T DET and DON'T DET.
sections.eli5: It teaches two computers to share a pretend form-filling terminal, so any real terminal can be mapped onto the same pretend one.

sections.title: Negotiating Facilities
sections.content:
After the usual IAC WILL DET or IAC DO DET exchange, the two sides use four facility subcommands, each carrying a bit map: edit (1), erase (2), transmit (3) and format (4). A server must send a facility subcommand before first using any subcommand or attribute outside the minimal implementation. The terminal side replies with the facilities it provides, and the requester takes the logical intersection of the two maps to learn what was agreed. For the intensity attribute it takes the minimum of the two numbers.

The minimal implementation covers the four facility subcommands, MOVE CURSOR, HOME, ERASE SCREEN, TRANSMIT SCREEN, FORMAT DATA and ERROR, and also requires the Output Line Width and Output Page Size options.
sections.eli5: First the two computers swap lists of tricks they know. They then use only the tricks that appear on both lists.

sections.title: Cursor, Erase, Transmit and Format Subcommands
sections.content:
Subcommands are numbered 1 to 41 in Appendix 1. Editing subcommands move the cursor by absolute address (MOVE CURSOR on a finite plane), by toroidal skips, or by UP, DOWN, LEFT and RIGHT, and insert or delete lines and characters. Transmit subcommands ask for the whole screen, unprotected fields, a line, a field, the rest of the screen, line or field, or modified fields. Erase subcommands clear similar regions.

FORMAT DATA gives the next count characters attributes such as blinking, reverse video, right justification, intensity and a protection level (none, protected, alphabetic only or numeric only). ERROR reports problems, with the philosophy that the implementation should still do its best to carry out the intent. Twelve error codes are listed in Appendix 2.
sections.eli5: There are messages for moving a pointer around the screen, wiping parts of it, painting fields with colors and locks, and sending back what the person typed.

sections.title: A Sample Form and the Byte Macro Appendix
sections.content:
The sample interaction negotiates the screen size (25 lines by 80 characters), sets terminal attributes, erases the screen and paints a protected form with fields for name, address, telephone number and a hidden Social Security Number field, then sends the cursor home. After the user fills it in, the terminal sends the unprotected data, with the fields separated by a macro byte.

Appendix 3 admits the main drawback of the option: because every function is a subnegotiation, a function like CHAR INSERT costs six bytes where most terminals use one. The Byte Macro Option (RFC 729) can map such strings to a single byte, and the appendix suggests choosing macro bytes by adding the subcommand code to 128.
sections.eli5: The example shows a computer drawing a paper-style form on your screen with some boxes locked, and then getting back only the boxes you filled in.
